sentences.text: Avisaurus is a genus of enantiornithine birds that lived during the Late Cretaceous in North America.
This was a large enantiornithine, with the species A. darwini weighing up to 1.2 kg and A. archibaldi weighing up to 1.7 kg.
Avisaurus possessed inwardly curved claws resembling those of eudromaeosaurs, indicating it was a predator.
The bird likely preyed on other vertebrates, showing similarities to modern raptors.

The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — of Avisaurus archibaldi was collected in 1975 in Garfield County, Montana, USA, and is a single fossil tarsometatarsus held by the University of California Museum of Paleontology. The species name archibaldi honors J. David Archibald, its discoverer from the University of California, Berkeley.
In 2024, a second species, Avisaurus darwini, was named from the Hell Creek Formation, with the specific name honoring Charles Darwin.
A species originally named Avisaurus gloriae from Montana was renamed Gettyia by Atterholt et al. in 2018.
Avisaurus belongs to the enantiornithine family Avisauridae, which includes similar animals from South America like Soroavisaurus, Neuquenornis, and Intiornis.
Avisaurus lived during the Maastrichtian stage, from 72.2 to 66 million years ago.
Avisaurus fossils are found in humid low-lying swamps, lakes, and river basins along the western shore of the Western Interior Seaway.
Fossils are also known from humid low-lying swamps, lakes, and river basins on the western shore of the Niobrara Sea, as well as from drier highlands between that area and the Overthrust Belt.
At the end of the Cretaceous, the Americas were separated by an arm of the Tethys Sea.

The reported presence of Avisaurus in both North and South America has been used as evidence that faunal changes in southern North America during the Lanciano were the result of an immigration event of South American taxa moving north.
